AI.method: We extend existing point-mass disruption constraints to include spherical extended dark objects, applying this framework to wide-binary candidates in Bootes I and analyzing their response to different mass-density models.
AI.result: We establish 95% confidence limits on dark matter fractions, showing significant sensitivity to these fractions even below unity, especially as perturber size and density profiles vary.
AI.conclusion: Ultra-faint-dwarf wide binaries serve as effective gravitational probes, revealing information about the abundance of extended dark matter objects and informing our understanding of the small-scale primordial curvature power spectrum.

title: The Norton Theorem for Quantum Circuits and Systems
summary: It is well known that classical analog circuits and systems benefit from the powerful Thevenin and Norton theorems. These theorems enable rigorous and exact mathematical simplification and representation of the effect of the rest of a system on the part we want to focus on. We show that there are corresponding versions of a "Quantum Norton Theorem" that enable exact simplification and reduction for quantum circuits and systems, not just for one port, but also for multiport and even open quantum systems. We demonstrate the method on two level systems, chains, system environment partitions, Lindblad examples, and Grover search. The Grover examples show how the reduced network isolates the bright pole governing ideal search and exposes how diagonal disorder transfers spectral weight into dark poles that degrade performance. By partitioning finite dimensional Schrodinger dynamics into retained and eliminated sectors, we show that Gaussian elimination gives an exact reduced equation in which the eliminated subsystem appears as a dynamical self energy and a source term. In the circuit representation, these terms become the Norton admittance and Norton current source seen by the retained quantum port. The same Schur complement construction extends to multiport reductions, composite system environment partitions, density matrix dynamics, and Lindblad evolution in Liouville space.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a Quantum Norton Theorem that simplifies reduction for quantum circuits, similar to classical theorems, demonstrating its application across various quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To provide rigorous mathematical tools for simplifying complex quantum circuits and systems, akin to classical Thevenin and Norton theorems.
AI.method: Develops a Quantum Norton Theorem enabling exact simplification, applied to multiport and open quantum systems. Utilizes Gaussian elimination and Schur complement methods for reduced equations.
AI.result: Showcases applications including two-level systems, environmental partitions, and Grover search, revealing the impact of diagonal disorder on performance and isolating dynamics relevant to ideal search.
AI.conclusion: The Quantum Norton Theorem offers a powerful framework for analyzing quantum systems, extending classical circuit principles to multiport and open quantum environments.

title: Correlated comagnetometry for precision measurements
summary: Magnetometers are among the most widely used probes in science and technology. Comagnetometers increase sensitivity by self-cancellation of magnetic noise, but only at low frequencies. We suggest a correlated measurement of two alkali species in one cell to cancel the magnetic background also at high frequencies. The inter-species phase difference of the light-matter interaction response function is found to be calibration free and insensitive to common-mode intensity noise. Utilizing a dark-matter signal as a testcase, the method achieves a thirtyfold background suppression, raising the signal-to-noise ratio by an order of magnitude or more, depending on the coupling to the different subatomic particles. We show that the method also provides model differentiation. The higher sensitivity and model differentiation open a path to novel probes for precision measurements in general and exotic fields in particular.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel method of using co-magnetometers with two alkali species for enhanced sensitivity in magnetic field measurements, achieving significant background noise suppression and improved signal-to-noise ratios, especially for detecting dark matter.
AI.motivation: To enhance the sensitivity of magnetometers which are limited by magnetic noise, particularly at high frequencies, and to improve measurement precision in physics and related fields.
AI.method: The authors propose a correlated measurement approach using two different alkali species in a single cell, leveraging the inter-species phase difference to cancel magnetic background noise across a wider frequency range.
AI.result: The method demonstrates a thirtyfold suppression of background noise and improves the signal-to-noise ratio by an order of magnitude or more, with variable gains depending on particle coupling.
AI.conclusion: This technique not only enhances measurement sensitivity but also allows for model differentiation, paving the way for advanced probes in precision measurements and exploration of exotic phenomena.

title: Sample-based quantum diagonalization approach for open-shell transition-metal complexes in gas and implicit-solvent
summary:
Open-shell $3d$ transition-metal complexes challenge electronic-structure methods because competing spin states, charge transfer, and solvation jointly determine their energetics. Here, we combine sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) with the integral-equation-formalism polarizable continuum model (IEF-PCM), extending SQD to correlated open-shell transition-metal systems in a dielectric environment.
  We investigate the octahedrally coordinated $\mathrm{[Co(H_2O)_5CO_2]^{2+/3+}}$ complex across two oxidation states, four spin multiplicities, and a metal-ligand dissociation coordinate. We study the Co(III) singlet and quintet states and the Co(II) doublet and quartet states, incorporating open-shell references into SQD-IEF-PCM through an outer self-consistent reaction-field loop. Using samples collected on an IBM Heron quantum processor and active spaces of up to 50 qubits, SQD reproduces coupled-cluster and heat-bath configuration-interaction benchmarks within the same active space in the gas phase and implicit solvent, with a largest observed deviation below 9 $mE_h$. Along the dissociation coordinate of high-spin quintet $\mathrm{[Co(H_2O)_5CO_2]^{3+}}$, SQD resolves an avoided crossing caused by internal charge transfer; this feature is absent in the singlet and the lower oxidation state of the complex. Relative to the gas phase, implicit solvation stabilizes for the quintet state the neutral CO$_2$ dissociation and suppresses the avoided-crossing feature.
  To our knowledge, this is the first hardware demonstration of SQD for an open-shell $3d$ transition-metal complex in gas phase and implict solvent. These results establish SQD as a robust quantum-centric approach for transition-metal chemistry where spin state ordering, charge transfer, and environmental effects are strongly intertwined.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a novel method combining sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) and the IEF-PCM for studying open-shell $	ext{3d}$ transition-metal complexes, specifically $	ext{[Co(H}_2	ext{O)}_5	ext{CO}_2]^{2+/3+}$, across various oxidation states and spin multiplicities in both gas and solvent phases.
AI.motivation: Open-shell $	ext{3d}$ transition-metal complexes present significant challenges in electronic structure calculations due to competing spin states and charge transfer effects, necessitating advanced methodologies.
AI.method: The study extends SQD to open-shell systems in a dielectric environment, utilizing an outer self-consistent reaction-field loop, implemented on an IBM Heron quantum processor with up to 50 qubits.
AI.result: SQD effectively reproduces benchmarks of coupled-cluster and heat-bath configuration-interaction methods, achieving deviations below 9 $mE_h$. It also identifies an avoided crossing from charge transfer in the high-spin state, influenced by solvation effects.
AI.conclusion: This work marks the first hardware implementation of SQD for open-shell $	ext{3d}$ transition-metal complexes, validating it as a promising approach for tackling the complexities of transition-metal chemistry.

title: HyperIso: A general BSM calculator for flavour observables
comment: 50 pages, 8 figures, 34 tables, source code can be obtained from https://hyperiso.in2p3.fr/
summary: We present HyperIso, a new standalone program for the evaluation of flavour physics observables across a wide variety of Standard Model (SM) and Beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) scenarios. The code builds on the physics heritage of SuperIso, but is implemented as a new modular software package with a modern C++ core and multiple user interfaces. In addition to native implementations for established scenarios such as the SM, the general Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (THDM), and supersymmetric models, HyperIso interfaces with the MARTY framework to compute automatically BSM Wilson coefficients at leading order. This design makes it possible to study user-defined BSM models while keeping the observable calculation, uncertainty propagation and statistical interpretation in a common backend. The software provides C++, Python, command-line and graphical interfaces. It supports the evaluation of key observables such as the branching ratios and, where available, angular observables, for radiative, leptonic, and semileptonic B decays, as well as for the relevant kaon and D-meson decays, together with the muon anomalous magnetic moment (g-2). The inputs can be provided through JSON/YAML configuration files and Les Houches Accord files, either supplied by the user or generated by external spectrum calculators. HyperIso therefore provides a flexible and extensible tool for flavour studies, phenomenological scans and the validation of BSM scenarios.

AI.tldr: HyperIso is a new software for evaluating flavour physics observables in both Standard Model and Beyond-the-Standard-Model scenarios, featuring modular design, modern interfaces, and integration with existing frameworks.
AI.motivation: To provide a versatile tool for assessing flavour observables across various particle physics models, enhancing analysis capabilities.
AI.method: HyperIso is a modular C++ program that interfaces with the MARTY framework for computing BSM Wilson coefficients, supporting multiple input formats, and allowing customizable user-defined scenarios.
AI.result: The software can evaluate key observables like branching ratios and angular observables for various particle decays, enhancing the analysis of both SM and BSM models.
AI.conclusion: HyperIso offers a flexible tool for flavour physics studies, enabling effective phenomenological scans and validation of BSM theories.

title: Dissipative Stabilization of Floquet-Engineered Many-Body Order
summary: Floquet driving underlies Hamiltonian and gate engineering, and produces dynamical orders with no equilibrium counterpart. These phenomena are, however, transient in well-isolated systems. We show that statically coupled dissipative auxiliaries cool the system toward low-energy states of the Floquet-engineered Hamiltonian, stabilizing orders in the steady state. The excess energy density is controllably small at high drive frequency and weak coupling and is captured by rate theory based on Fermi's Golden Rule. We numerically confirm robust cooling in a Floquet-engineered transverse-field Ising chain in both phases, and demonstrate discrete time-crystalline order, with a period-doubled magnetization response, in the steady state of a long-range Ising chain. Our results provide a rare analytical handle on the steady states of driven dissipative systems.

AI.tldr: Investigation into Floquet driving highlights the stabilization of dynamical orders in dissipative systems through auxiliary cooling.
AI.motivation: To address the transient nature of dynamical orders produced by Floquet driving in well-isolated systems.
AI.method: Employing statically coupled dissipative auxiliaries to cool the system toward low-energy states and using rate theory based on Fermi's Golden Rule to analyze energy density.
AI.result: Numerical confirmation of robust cooling in a Floquet-engineered transverse-field Ising chain and observation of discrete time-crystalline order in a long-range Ising chain.
AI.conclusion: Provides analytical insights into the steady states of driven dissipative systems, enhancing the understanding of dynamically stabilized orders.

title: Theoretical uncertainties in reconstructing model parameters with gravitational waves from supercooled phase transitions
summary: Future interferometers may detect a gravitational-wave (GW) signal from a cosmological first-order phase transition. Reconstructing the underlying particle-physics model from such a signal requires theoretical control over the map from microphysics to the spectrum. For classically scale-invariant extensions of the Standard Model, which generically predict strongly supercooled transitions and strong GW signals, this map depends sensitively on the treatment of quantum and thermal corrections to the nucleation rate. Taking the classically conformal ${\rm U}(1)_X$ model as representative of this class, we scan its parameter space and compare two resummation schemes. The first is a high-temperature effective field theory, matched at two-loop level and including next-to-leading-order corrections to the bounce action, with the nucleation-rate prefactor given by the full one-loop functional determinants. The second is a commonly employed daisy-resummed effective potential, with the prefactor estimated on dimensional grounds. Reconstructing the fundamental model parameters through a Fisher-matrix analysis of injected GW signals at LISA, we find that the daisy-resummation scheme is strongly disfavored, as its theoretical error dominates over the reconstruction uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The study analyzes gravitational-wave signals from cosmological phase transitions, comparing two resummation methods in a classically conformal ${\rm U}(1)_X$ model. It finds the daisy-resummation scheme is less reliable for reconstructing fundamental model parameters due to higher theoretical error.
AI.motivation: Understanding gravitational-wave signals from cosmological phase transitions can help reconstruct particle-physics models, specifically in classically scale-invariant extensions of the Standard Model.
AI.method: The paper compares a high-temperature effective field theory approach and a daisy-resummed effective potential for calculating the nucleation rate of phase transitions in the ${\rm U}(1)_X$ model.
AI.result: The daisy-resummation scheme was found to introduce significant theoretical errors that overshadow the uncertainties in reconstructing parameters from gravitational-wave data, particularly for injected signals analyzed via Fisher-matrix methods.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that for accurate model reconstruction from gravitational waves, the use of daisy-resummation is strongly disfavored due to its detrimental impact on theoretical precision.

title: Entanglement Entropy in Quantum Networks with Tunable Geometry
summary: Quantum many-body Hamiltonians with two-body interactions can be represented by graphs, with sites as nodes and two-site couplings as edges. We investigate how the geometry of these graphs affects transport and entanglement growth. To do so, we study dynamics for quantum hopping on a random graph model with an effective range parameter. Tuning it, we interpolate between nearest-neighbor and all-to-all graphs, identifying a new localization regime that is robust in both single-particle and finite-density cases. This provides a model of Anderson localization induced by structural disorder, with implications for amorphous materials and tunable-range analog quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: The study explores the impact of graph geometry on transport and entanglement in quantum many-body systems, revealing a new localization regime amidst varied interaction ranges.
AI.motivation: Understanding how the structure of quantum systems affects behavior, particularly in disordered environments, is crucial for applications in quantum simulation and material science.
AI.method: The dynamics of quantum hopping on a tunable random graph model were analyzed, varying the effective range of interactions between nearest-neighbor and all-to-all configurations.
AI.result: A novel localization regime was discovered that applies to both single-particle and finite-density scenarios, indicating robustness against structural disorder.
AI.conclusion: The findings have significant implications for understanding Anderson localization in disordered systems and for developing tunable-range quantum simulators.

title: How many degrees of freedom describe a quantum N-particle state?
comment: 30 pages of main text, 25 pages of appendices, and 8 pages of references. No tables, no figures
summary: In Newtonian spacetime, the canonical description of a classical $N$-particle system requires $3N$ degrees of freedom. Not all of these are physical, however, since the conservation of the net momentum implies that only $3(N-1)$ accelerations are independent. Hence, three constraints can be used to eliminate the unphysical centre-of-mass variables, at the level of the Lagrangian, leaving only the subset of observable displacements and momenta, which are relational. Imposing the constraints does not change the dynamics of these variables, at the classical level, and is analogous to a gauge-fixing procedure, which removes redundancy in the description of the system. In classical physics, therefore, the number of physical degrees of freedom equals the number of independent relational degrees of freedom. Here, we show that this is not the case in quantum mechanics. While an operator-analogue of the classical net momentum exists, it cannot be used to impose constraints that restrict the degrees of freedom in the theory, without a loss of physical information. This means that all $3N$ canonical degrees of freedom are physical, even though only $3(N-1)$ of them are relational. We explore the physical consequences of the non-relational variables and show that they give rise to generalised uncertainty relations (GURs), for the relational quantities that define the quantum reference frame (QRF). Hence, it is shown that the non-relational degrees of freedom refer to the frame itself and that the non-Heisenberg terms in the GURs define its Galilean-invariant spreads, in both real space and momentum space. The implications of this result for recent work on relational models, including the ``perspective neutral'' framework for QRFs, are discussed. Its implications for the wider relational program, and, in particular, the relevance of the latter to quantum gravity research, are also critically assessed

AI.tldr: This paper contrasts classical and quantum mechanics in the treatment of degrees of freedom in $N$-particle systems, revealing that while classical mechanics restricts physical degrees of freedom via gauge-fixing, quantum mechanics retains all degrees as physical, leading to unique uncertainty relations.
AI.motivation: The study aims to clarify the discrepancies between classical and quantum treatments of particle systems, particularly regarding the nature of degrees of freedom and their relational aspects.
AI.method: The authors analyze the degrees of freedom in classical Newtonian spacetime and explore the implications of non-relational variables in quantum mechanics, leading to the derivation of generalized uncertainty relations (GURs).
AI.result: The findings indicate that in quantum mechanics, all $3N$ degrees of freedom are physical, despite only $3(N-1)$ being relational. This leads to GURs that highlight the role of non-relational variables related to the quantum reference frame (QRF).
AI.conclusion: The paper suggests that non-relational degrees of freedom have significant implications for relational models and quantum gravity research, redefining understandings of physical degrees of freedom in quantum contexts.

title: Uncountably many inequivalent maximally entangled measurements for two qutrits
summary: Every two-qubit measurement basis composed of maximally entangled eigenstates can be transformed into the Bell basis via local unitary operations. For higher dimensions, in contrast, there exist inequivalent bases composed of maximally entangled eigenstates. Here, we provide a single-parameter family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases, and demonstrate that none of the bases are equivalent to each other under local unitaries. These bases are constructed from the continuous family of symmetric informationally complete sets of states in dimension three. By studying the local unitary bases that generate the family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases, we construct the first examples of wild error bases in the smallest dimension where these can exist. Finally, we discuss how distinct measurements in the family lead to differences in performance in several scenarios relevant in quantum information.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a single-parameter family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases that are not equivalent under local unitary operations, highlighting their differences in quantum information applications.
AI.motivation: To explore the structure of maximally entangled states in higher dimensions, particularly focusing on two-qutrit systems and their measurement bases.
AI.method: The authors construct a continuous family of symmetric informationally complete sets in dimension three and analyze the local unitary operations that lead to inequivalent two-qutrit measurement bases.
AI.result: The study finds that none of the constructed two-qutrit maximally entangled bases are equivalent under local unitaries, providing the first examples of wild error bases in this dimension.
AI.conclusion: Distinct measurements within this family can lead to varying performance in quantum information scenarios, emphasizing the importance of understanding these inequivalent bases.

title: Quantum-Centric Geometry Optimization with Wave-Function-Based Embedding
summary: The EWF-(FCI,SQD) method, a wave-function-based embedding approach combining full configuration interaction (FCI) and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), is a promising new tool for the simulation of molecular systems. However, applications of EWF-(FCI,SQD) have so far been limited to single-point calculations, whereas the study of complex chemical processes requires the ability to explore potential energy surfaces. In this work, we demonstrate geometry optimization with EWF-(FCI,SQD), scaling our simulations to molecules as large as menthone and benzidine within the STO-3G basis set. Without fragmentation, these systems comprise 73 and 82 molecular orbitals respectively, presenting an intractable Hilbert space for conventional exact or high-level subspace solvers and establishing a clear necessity for fragmentation-based methodologies. The underlying fragment SQD simulations in the EWF-(FCI,SQD) geometry optimizations use up to 70 qubits. The resulting geometries show exceptional accuracy relative to the classical reference, with deviations below 4 picometers.

AI.tldr: The EWF-(FCI,SQD) method enhances molecular simulations by enabling geometry optimization for larger molecules, achieving high accuracy.
AI.motivation: The EWF-(FCI,SQD) method is developed to address limitations in current simulation methods that only allow single-point calculations, which are inadequate for studying complex chemical processes requiring exploration of potential energy surfaces.
AI.method: This work implements the EWF-(FCI,SQD) method for geometry optimization, applying it to larger molecular systems without fragmentation, such as menthone and benzidine, and employing up to 70 qubits in fragment SQD simulations.
AI.result: The geometry optimization results demonstrate exceptional accuracy with deviations from classical references being under 4 picometers, validating the method's effectiveness for larger molecules.
AI.conclusion: The successful application of EWF-(FCI,SQD) for geometry optimization in sizable molecular systems showcases its potential and highlights the importance of fragmentation-based methodologies in quantum simulations.

title: Remote Infrared Absorption Spectroscopy with Undetected Photons
summary: We demonstrate a novel method for remote open-path Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy with undetected photons. Similar to previous quantum spectroscopy works, a mid-infrared spectrum is reconstructed by detecting a near-infrared radiation only, thus bypassing important limitations of infrared detectors. Our study however relies on the co-propagation of the photon-pair and the pump-laser over the same optical path, which allows the probing of the open atmosphere over long distances. By sending the photons over unprecedented distances of up-to 43.4m in the outdoor atmosphere, we were able to detect butane released in the open-path, as well as natural atmospheric methane, thus demonstrating the first use of infrared spectroscopy with undetected photons for atmospheric measurements.

AI.tldr: This study introduces a method for remote infrared spectroscopy using undetected photons, enabling long-distance atmospheric analysis without the limitations of traditional detectors.
AI.motivation: To overcome the limitations of conventional infrared detectors in open-path spectroscopy, particularly for atmospheric measurements.
AI.method: The method involves co-propagating photon pairs and a pump laser along the same optical path, allowing long-distance probing of the atmosphere.
AI.result: The authors successfully demonstrated detection of butane and natural atmospheric methane over distances of up to 43.4m in an outdoor environment.
AI.conclusion: This work marks the first application of infrared spectroscopy utilizing undetected photons for atmospheric analysis.

title: Feynman Meets Turing: The Curse of Quantum Universality
summary: We consider a formal model of quantum circuit description languages (QCDLs) in which semantically meaningful programs correspond to computable unitary matrices. We show that any semantically universal QCDL -- that is, any QCDL able to describe all computable unitary matrices, which in turn form the set of matrices we can meaningfully represent on digital hardware -- cannot have a semi-decidable set of semantically meaningful descriptions. In particular, no such language admits a compiler that reliably recognizes all valid program descriptions. This result stands in contrast to classical programming languages. While compilation in languages such as C or C++ may itself involve non-terminating computations, the set of semantically meaningful programs remains recursively enumerable, since successful compilation provides a witness of validity. The essential difference lies in the nature of the semantic domains: classical languages describe partial recursive functions, whereas QCDLs describe total unitary operators. Our analysis establishes a fundamental limitation of quantum circuit description languages and highlights a structural distinction between classical and quantum models of computation at the level of formal language theory.

AI.tldr: Quantum circuit description languages (QCDLs) cannot have a semi-decidable set of valid programs, distinguishing them from classical programming languages where such a set is recursively enumerable.
AI.motivation: The study explores the formal limitations of QCDLs in representing all computable unitary matrices, essential for quantum computation.
AI.method: A formal model of QCDLs is analyzed to examine the properties of semi-decidability and compilation consistency in relation to unitary matrices.
AI.result: It is shown that no semantically universal QCDL admits a compiler that can reliably recognize all valid program descriptions, in contrast to classical languages.
AI.conclusion: This work highlights a fundamental limitation of QCDLs and a structural distinction between classical and quantum computation within formal language theory.

title: Host-guest Crystal Engineering Tailors the Room Temperature Spin Dynamics in Molecular Quantum Devices
summary: Molecular materials that enable coherent control over an electron's spin state at room temperature are promising candidates for quantum technologies, including quantum sensors and ultra-low noise microwave amplifiers, known as masers. Host-guest molecular crystals enable independent control of spin-active guests and their local environments to enhance molecular spin properties and so improve device performance. Using electron paramagnetic resonance and optically-detected magnetic resonance, we demonstrate the ability to tune triplet population, depopulation, and spin-lattice relaxation by modulating host-dependent lattice rigidity and vibrational coupling to significantly reduce the operating requirements for building useful masers. Importantly, the most rigid host, picene, reveals the ability to slow spin-lattice relaxation without lengthening triplet lifetime, though at the cost of strain-induced line width broadening and reduced triplet spin polarisation. We also find that deuteration reduces the triplet resonance line width and vibrationally-mediated triplet depopulation. Consequently, we find that perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl is the most viable candidate for building a continuous wave maser. This work demonstrates host-guest engineering as an important and practical method for tuning the spin-dependent performance of room-temperature molecular quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: This paper explores host-guest molecular crystals to enhance electron spin control at room temperature for improved quantum technologies, presenting findings on spin relaxation and depopulation mechanisms and identifying a prime candidate for masers.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to develop molecular materials that facilitate coherent electron spin control at room temperature for applications in quantum technologies like sensors and microwave amplifiers.
AI.method: Using electron paramagnetic resonance and optically-detected magnetic resonance, the study investigates how host-dependent lattice rigidity and vibrational coupling affect triplet population, depopulation, and spin-lattice relaxation.
AI.result: The most rigid host, picene, slows spin-lattice relaxation without extending triplet lifetime, though it leads to strain-induced linewidth broadening and decreased spin polarization. Deuteration also reduces resonance line width and enhances triplet retention.
AI.conclusion: Perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl emerges as the best candidate for continuous wave masers, highlighting host-guest engineering as a key technique in optimizing room-temperature molecular quantum technologies.

title: Holographic quantum codes with trapped ions
summary: Holography is a central concept at the intersection of gravity, condensed matter theory, and quantum information, linking the interior bulk of a system to its boundary. A model realizing key features of holographic systems is the holographic pentagon code by Pastawski et al. Here we experimentally implement instances of the holographic pentagon and heptagon codes with trapped ions and test their properties: For the pentagon code, we recover logical bulk qubits from their nearby boundary and test the Ryu-Takayanagi entanglement area law. For the heptagon code, we show that the transversal Hadamard gate native to the constituent Steane codes induces a single-qubit, correctable error in the holographic code. Our implementation paves the way towards the use of holographic quantum codes for quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: The paper experimentally implements holographic pentagon and heptagon codes using trapped ions, exploring their properties and potential for quantum information processing.
AI.motivation: The study aims to link gravity, condensed matter theory, and quantum information through holography, enhancing understanding of holographic systems.
AI.method: The authors experimentally implement the holographic pentagon and heptagon codes with trapped ions, testing the retrieval of logical bulk qubits and the effects of Hadamard gates on errors in the heptagon code.
AI.result: For the pentagon code, logical bulk qubits are successfully recovered and the Ryu-Takayanagi entanglement area law is validated. The heptagon code demonstrates a correctable single-qubit error induced by the Hadamard gate.
AI.conclusion: The findings advance the application of holographic quantum codes in quantum information processing, suggesting practical implications for future research.

title: Split-quaternionic structure and canonical quantization of the Bateman dual oscillator
summary: Bateman's dual oscillator embeds a damped harmonic oscillator and an independent anti-damped adjoint coordinate in a conservative doubled system. We develop a split-quaternionic formulation that remains consistent from the classical equations through ordinary complex canonical quantization. The doubled dynamics is written as a two-sided hypercomplex evolution whose conserved indefinite quadratic form is the split norm, while the sign of the generator square unifies the underdamped, overdamped, and critical regimes. The Bateman Lagrangian is recovered as a real scalar action on the split-complex configuration subalgebra. After quantization, operator-valued split quaternions belong to the complexified algebra $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb H_s\simeq M_2(\mathbb C)$. Noncommuting mechanical components require a symmetrized quantum split norm, which exactly reproduces the symmetrically ordered canonical Hamiltonian. Null idempotents resolve the crossed canonical structure of the doubled phase space. In particular, damping yields $[m\dot{\widehat y},m\dot{\widehat x}]=\mathrm{i}\hbar mγ$ and a Robertson--Schrödinger uncertainty relation. The limit $γ\to0$ retains the doubled positive/negative geometry; the ordinary single-oscillator Heisenberg relation is recovered only after selecting the positive normal mode, or by undoubling before quantization. The scalar split action gives the exact quadratic propagator and Gaussian evolution. A formal trace over the auxiliary coordinate is finally compared with high-temperature Caldeira--Leggett dynamics, clarifying that the doubled model is a coherent zero-noise embedding rather than a microscopic reservoir theory.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a dual oscillator model using a split-quaternionic approach, addressing classical and quantum dynamics, with implications for understanding damping and uncertainty relations.
AI.motivation: To explore the dynamics of dual oscillators and establish a coherent framework for understanding quantum properties through a novel mathematical formulation.
AI.method: Utilizes a split-quaternionic formulation to describe a damped harmonic oscillator system, employing hypercomplex evolution and operator-valued entities to analyze quantum behavior.
AI.result: Demonstrates that the model encompasses various damping regimes, reproduces canonical Hamiltonian relations, and highlights a coherent embedding in zero-noise dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The study bridges classical and quantum descriptions of oscillators, revealing insights into propagation, evolution, and uncertainty, with implications beyond mere microscopic reservoir theory.

title: Efficient Exact Quantum Sampling from the Sun-Wootters Distribution for Optimal Polynomial Intersection
summary: Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) is a structured optimization problem for which Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) attains a satisfaction guarantee governed by the semicircle law. Sun and Wootters recently showed that, for balanced OPI over prime fields, a Fourier-defined distribution $P_u$ gives a strict worst-case improvement from limiting rate $0.6225$ onward and asymptotically perfect solutions from rate $0.7496$ onward, and asked whether $P_u$ can be sampled efficiently. We answer this question for Reed--Solomon OPI parameters satisfying their exponent condition strictly below the dual Johnson radius. Under coherent membership-oracle access, we give a bounded-error polynomial-time quantum sampler for $P_u$. The ideal circuit samples $P_u$ exactly conditioned on success, while a finite-precision implementation achieves any prescribed inverse-polynomial total-variation error. Consequently, every fixed limiting rate $0.6225\le r<1$ admits a strict worst-case improvement over the DQI semicircle value, and every limiting rate $r\ge 3/4$ admits solutions of satisfaction $1-o(1)$ with high probability. The algorithm coherently sums the amplitudes of all low-weight errors in each syndrome class using deterministic complete list decoding. Complete Reed--Solomon list decoding and the Sun--Wootters denominator estimate make the list size and postselection overhead polynomial. In concurrent and independent work, Horinaga and Yamakawa obtain worst-case OPI algorithms over prime-power fields and exact satisfaction at every fixed rate strictly above $3/4$.

AI.tldr: A quantum sampling method is developed for Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problems, showing improvements in performance based on defined rates, while ensuring efficient execution under specific conditions.
AI.motivation: The need to improve sampling efficiency for Fourier-defined distributions in OPI, particularly under the constraints set forth by the semicircle law and existing limitations in previous works.
AI.method: A polynomial-time quantum sampler is proposed under coherent membership-oracle access, enabling exact sampling of a defined distribution $P_u$ with bounded error.
AI.result: The sampler demonstrates that any limiting rate from $0.6225$ to $1$ yields better worst-case performance compared to the DQI semicircle value, with high probability satisfaction as rates approach $3/4$.
AI.conclusion: The work confirms that efficient sampling for limited-rate scenarios enhances outcomes in OPI and complements concurrent findings in related research.

title: Quantum dynamics of a levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope
summary: We develop a quantum model for the rotational dynamics of a freely floating levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope (LFG), emphasizing the interplay between intrinsic spin $\boldsymbol{S}$, mechanical angular momentum $\boldsymbol{L}$, and magnetic torque. The conserved total angular momentum projection along the $z$-directed magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}$, $J_z=S_z+L_z$, is quantized, leading in the small-libration-amplitude limit to discrete precessional states $|m\rangle$ (eigenstates of $J_z$ with eigenvalues $J_z = m\hbar$) and librational harmonic oscillator states $|n\rangle$ ($n=0,1,2,\ldots$). The discreteness of the energies and dynamical variables is governed by the quantum precession scale $Ω_Q=\hbar/I$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia of the LFG. We find that the phenomenon of LFG precession persists into high-field regimes where the magnitude of the rotational angular momentum associated with precession exceeds the total intrinsic spin. We analyze the complementary quantum limits of localized semiclassical LFG orientation wave packets and exact $J_z$-eigenstates $|m\rangle$, clarifying the relation between classical precession signals and the underlying quantized spin-rotor dynamics. We further show that radio-frequency fields can drive $Δm = \pm 1$ and $Δn = \pm 1$ transitions, enabling ladder spectroscopy, tilt-angle control, and sideband-like coupling between precession and libration. The coupled dynamics also exhibit branch-point magnetic resonances where precession and librational motion become strongly coupled. These results establish a framework for using LFGs not only as ultrasensitive torque and magnetic-field sensors, but also as controllable mesoscopic quantum systems. The techniques developed here may be applied to searches for exotic, beyond-the-standard model spin-dependent interactions, ultralight dark matter, and spin-gravity couplings.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a quantum model for the rotational dynamics of a levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope, focusing on the interaction between spin, angular momentum, and magnetic torque. It explores discrete precessional states, the persistence of gyroscope precession, transitions driven by radio-frequency fields, and implications for advanced sensing and fundamental physics.
AI.motivation: The study aims to establish a quantum framework for understanding the rotational dynamics of levitated ferromagnetic gyroscopes and their potential applications in sensing and fundamental physics.
AI.method: A quantum model is developed that quantizes the total angular momentum and analyzes the dynamics of precessional and librational states under magnetic torque and radio-frequency fields.
AI.result: The model shows that the gyroscope's precessional states persist even under high magnetic field strengths, with discrete energy levels and dynamic coupling between precession and libration. The research includes observations on transitions driven by external fields and the strong coupling of precessional and librational motions.
AI.conclusion: The findings lay the groundwork for utilizing levitated ferromagnetic gyroscopes as ultra-sensitive sensors and controllable quantum systems, with applications in detecting various fundamental interactions.

title: Geometric quantum discord in the black hole quantum atmosphere
summary: We investigate the geometric quantum discord of bipartite Werner states influenced by Hawking radiation in the quantum atmosphere of a Schwarzschild black hole. We find that the geometric quantum discord in the physically accessible region exhibits a nonmonotonic behavior: it first decreases and then increases as the normalized radial distance increases, while the discord in the physically inaccessible region shows the exact opposite trend. A pronounced extremum of geometric quantum discord occurs precisely at the position corresponding to the peak intensity of Hawking radiation. Furthermore, we find that the Hartle Hawking constant and the event horizon radius exert opposite effects on the strength of quantum correlation redistribution: a larger Hartle Hawking constant enhances the redistribution effect, whereas a larger event horizon radius suppresses it.

AI.tldr: This study examines how Hawking radiation affects the geometric quantum discord of bipartite Werner states near a Schwarzschild black hole, revealing distinct behaviors in accessible and inaccessible regions.
AI.motivation: To understand the effects of Hawking radiation on quantum correlations in bipartite systems within the context of black hole physics.
AI.method: The study analyzes geometric quantum discord in bipartite Werner states influenced by Hawking radiation, examining variations based on radial distance from the black hole.
AI.result: Geometric quantum discord shows nonmonotonic behavior in the accessible region and opposite behavior in the inaccessible region; notably, the peak discord occurs where Hawking radiation is most intense.
AI.conclusion: The Hartle Hawking constant enhances quantum correlation redistribution, while a larger event horizon radius has a suppressive effect.

title: $p$-Body $\simeq$ Range $p-1$: Exact Order-Range Mapping and Dual-Unitarity
summary: We introduce and study a periodically kicked version of a one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ Ising model with contiguous $p$-body interactions. At specific interaction strengths of the model, we establish an exact Floquet interaction $\textit{order-range}$ mapping: the Floquet evolution operator of the $p$-body Ising model is exactly mapped to a two body Ising model with interactions having maximum range $p-1$ and exactly determined couplings. Upon further tuning the kicking strength, the mapped model becomes dual-unitary, thus providing an explicit family of $p$-body dual unitary models. We then determine exact entanglement dynamics of the $p$-body model for a class of solvable initial states at all times. We further illustrate the nontrivial structures that can emerge from the $\textit{order-range}$ mapping using a minimal example of $p=3$ and generalize it for all odd $p$. These findings provide a systematic route to constructing and studying $p$-body dual-unitary Floquet models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a periodically kicked version of a one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ Ising model with contiguous $p$-body interactions, revealing an exact mapping to a dual-unitary two-body Ising model and exploring the entanglement dynamics of the $p$-body model.
AI.motivation: To enhance the understanding of complex quantum systems through periodic driving and dual-unitarity, while exploring entanglement dynamics.
AI.method: The study establishes an exact Floquet interaction order-range mapping, linking the Floquet evolution of a $p$-body Ising model to a two-body Ising model with modified couplings, and analyzes entanglement dynamics for solvable initial states.
AI.result: The paper highlights that upon tuning the kicking strength, the model becomes dual-unitary, and nontrivial entanglement dynamics are determined for $p$-body interactions, specifically illustrating structures arising from the mapping for odd $p$.
AI.conclusion: The findings present a systematic approach for constructing and investigating $p$-body dual-unitary Floquet models, contributing significantly to the study of quantum entanglement and interacting systems.

title: Geometric Power Capacity of Coherent Ergotropy in Quantum Batteries
summary: We explore coherent ergotropy extraction in quantum batteries from a resource-geometric point of view. For an initial state $ρ$, we quantify the coherent extraction process by the coherent ergotropy $\mathcal{E}_c(ρ)$ and the coherent extraction distance $D_c^{\rm ext}(ρ)$ between the active state $σ_ρ$ and the passive state $P_ρ$. This defines the geometric power capacity $Π_c(ρ)=\mathcal{E}_c(ρ)/D_c^{\rm ext}(ρ)$, which measures the coherent ergotropy released unit minimal unitary distance. We prove that, for any driving Hamiltonian satisfying $\|V_t\|\leqν$, the actual coherent discharging power is bounded by $P_c^{\rm ext}(ρ;V_t)\leq νΠ_c(ρ)$, showing that $Π_c(ρ)$ is a capacity under unit driving norm rather than the power of a particular protocol. General bounds on $Π_c(ρ)$ are derived by combining relative entropy bounds on coherent ergotropy with geometric bounds on the coherent extraction distance. We also formulate coherence measure induced bounds and protocol-corrected capacities involving the effective speed of a given Hamiltonian. Qubit and qutrit examples demonstrate that $Π_c(ρ)$ captures a resource-geometric feature of coherent discharging beyond coherent ergotropy or coherence measures alone.

AI.tldr: The study quantifies coherent ergotropy extraction in quantum batteries using a geometric framework, introducing the concept of geometric power capacity and establishing bounds for coherent discharging power based on relative entropy and coherence measures.
AI.motivation: To analyze coherent ergotropy extraction in quantum batteries using a resource-geometric perspective, enhancing understanding of power capacities in quantum systems.
AI.method: The authors define coherent ergotropy and extraction distance, introducing geometric power capacity as a measure. They derive bounds on this capacity using relative entropy and geometric properties of coherent extraction distances.
AI.result: The study shows that the coherent discharging power is bounded by the geometric power capacity, establishing a framework that highlights the resource-geometric aspect of coherent energy extraction.
AI.conclusion: The geometric power capacity provides a deeper understanding of coherent discharging in quantum batteries, surpassing traditional measures of coherent ergotropy or coherence.

title: Mean-State Entropy Hierarchies and Classical Communication through Quantum Convolutions
summary: Quantum convolution provides a discrete-variable analogue of classical convolution, with the mean state capturing the stabilizer structure preserved under repeated convolution. We establish a finite-step entropy hierarchy generated by compatible stabilizer dephasings. Along every compatible isotropic flag, the entropy increases toward the mean-state entropy ceiling, while the relative-entropy distance to the mean state decomposes exactly into successive coherence losses and a terminal classical nonuniformity. Optimizing over compatible subspaces yields an intrinsic entropy profile of the state. For quantum convolutional channels, Weyl covariance reduces the one-shot classical communication problem to minimal output entropy. A spectral-transfer argument shows that suitable stabilizer inputs reproduce stabilizer-measurement distributions of the environment as channel-output spectra. This gives a computable Holevo lower bound over all complete stabilizer measurements; its compatible restriction is characterized by the entropy hierarchy and refines the previous mean-state bound of Bu, Gu, and Jaffe. The bound is exact for stabilizer-diagonal environments, for which the Holevo capacity is strongly additive, and yields a single-letter formula for a nonstabilizer qutrit family. The same family also exhibits a coexistence region with simultaneously positive classical and quantum communication rates

AI.tldr: The paper explores the properties of quantum convolution in relation to stabilizer structures and presents an entropy hierarchy that aids in understanding optimal communication strategies in quantum channels.
AI.motivation: To investigate the role of stabilizer structures in quantum convolution and their implications for classical communication limits in quantum channels.
AI.method: Establishes a finite-step entropy hierarchy through compatible stabilizer dephasings and analyzes the relationships between entropy, coherence losses, and classical nonuniformity in stabilizer states. Applies Weyl covariance to simplify classical communication problems in quantum convolutional channels.
AI.result: Introduces a computable Holevo lower bound for classical communication capacities in stabilizer channels, showing exactness under specific environments and refining existing bounds.
AI.conclusion: The entropy hierarchy demonstrates significant insights into optimal communication strategies in quantum channels, with specific applications to stabilizer-diagonal environments and establishes coexistence regions for communication rates.

title: Graph State Generation Based on Quantum Photonic Devices, Enabling Measurement-Based Quantum Computing
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Qualifying exam paper, originally presented March 2025
summary: Photonic cluster states are fundamental resource for measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC), which is a promising approach for scalable quantum computing. These highly entangled states enable computation with applying local measurements rather than gate operations, which makes them essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Generation of the photonic cluster states requires high-quality entanglement and stability, which can be done by making use of cavity quantum electrodynamics (cavity QED), which is embedding quantum dots (QDs) into photonic microcavities. This method enables controlled single-photon emission and the entanglement of them, helping with key challenges in generating photonic cluster states. Enhancing the generation of the photonic cluster state requires improvement in the quality factor (Q-factor) and therefore, cooperativity of cavity and QD systems. A high Q-factor helps with reduction in photon loss and decoherence, ensuring more stable and high-fidelity quantum states. It also enables better light-matter interactions, improving cluster state quality. Cooperativity, which is a measure for the light-matter coupling strength relative to dissipation, directly impacts photon emission efficiency. Optimization of these parameters improves entanglement generation, which is essential for producing high-quality photonic cluster states. Therefore, optimized cavities are essential for improving the generation of the photonic cluster states. Scalability is also an important parameter for the generation of the large-scale cluster states used in quantum computing. In this paper, after reviewing MBQC, cluster states, and the generation of the photonic cluster states, we investigate the deterministic generation of the photonic cluster state resource for the purpose of MBQC, and highlights the importance of the inverse design techniques for this goal.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the deterministic generation of photonic cluster states for measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC), focusing on the role of cavity quantum electrodynamics (cavity QED) and optimization techniques.
AI.motivation: The need for high-quality entangled states in measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) to ensure fault tolerance and scalability in quantum systems.
AI.method: Utilizing cavity quantum electrodynamics by embedding quantum dots in photonic microcavities to enhance the emission and entanglement of single photons, while optimizing quality factors and cooperativity.
AI.result: Enhanced generation of photonic cluster states through improved light-matter interactions and efficiency in photon emission, assisting in overcoming key challenges.
AI.conclusion: Optimized cavities and inverse design techniques are critical for scalable and stable generation of high-quality photonic cluster states necessary for MBQC.

title: A projection-free approach toward mapping the structured polarization fields
summary: We present a projection-free method for mapping two-dimensional polarization distributions using Hong-Ou -Mandel (HOM) interference. Conventional polarization characterization techniques, such as Stokes polarimetry, rely on sequential intensity measurements under multiple polarization projections, making their accuracy and sensitivity susceptible to the extinction ratio, calibration errors, and stability of the polarization analysis optics. Our approach overcomes these limitations by exploiting the sensitivity of two-photon bunching to polarization indistinguishability at a balanced beam splitter. Using a HOM interferometer driven by a high-brightness spontaneous parametric down-conversion photon-pair source at 810 nm, we introduced a birefringent vortex waveplate with spatially varying polarization rotations in one interferometer arm and measured the resulting coincidence counts with a high signal-to-noise ratio, enabling projection-free characterization of the sample-induced polarization transformations. This configuration maps spatially dependent polarization variations directly onto coincidence counts, providing a projection-free reconstruction of the polarization distribution. We demonstrate high-fidelity ($\sim$95$\%$) reconstruction of the spatial polarization pattern with an angular resolution of approximately $\sim0.4^\circ$. The use an estimator that saturates the Cramer-Rao bound, computed from the Fisher information, can improve resolution further at the cost of longer acquisition. The proposed quantum-optical technique offers a simple, scalable, and high-precision framework for characterizing structured polarization fields in birefringent materials.

AI.tldr: A projection-free method for mapping 2D polarization distributions using HOM interference is proposed, overcoming the limitations of traditional techniques.
AI.motivation: Conventional polarization characterization relies on multiple projections, which can lead to inaccuracies due to various optical errors.
AI.method: The method employs a HOM interferometer with a birefringent vortex waveplate to measure coincidence counts, enabling the mapping of polarization transformations without projections.
AI.result: Achieved a high-fidelity ($\sim$95$\%$) reconstruction of spatial polarization with an angular resolution of approximately $\sim0.4^\circ$.
AI.conclusion: This quantum-optical technique provides a simple, scalable, and high-precision framework for characterizing structured polarization fields in birefringent materials.

title: Quantum Metrological Detection of the Unruh Effect with Optimized Accelerated Two-Level Atoms
summary: For a uniformly accelerated two-level probe atom, the acceleration-dependent factor is encoded in the atomic state during the atom-field evolution. If this factor can be estimated through a large number of measurements with an uncertainty smaller than its magnitude, the Unruh effect can be experimentally verified. In this work, we show that the minimal uncertainty is inversely proportional to the square root of the total probe time. For a fixed total probe time, we minimize the estimation uncertainty by optimizing the atom-field interaction time, the initial atomic state, and the measurement basis in each probe. Results show that the uncertainty decreases as the evolution time of each individual probe becomes shorter. The optimal measurement basis is determined by the initial atomic state, while the optimal initial state depends on both the acceleration factor and the evolution time of each probe. For a fixed evolution time, we analyze the estimation uncertainty versus the acceleration factor and identify the optimal factor and minimal uncertainty for each initial state. The initial excited state outperforms other configurations in the small-acceleration regime, whereas the ground state can become advantageous for sufficiently large acceleration and long evolution time of each probe. Finally, we estimate the minimal total probe time required for testing the Unruh effect and demonstrate that it can be significantly reduced by using probe atoms with larger transition dipole moments.

AI.tldr: This paper explores how to experimentally verify the Unruh effect through optimal measurement techniques in a uniformly accelerated two-level atom setup, focusing on minimizing uncertainty in estimations.
AI.motivation: The Unruh effect suggests that an accelerating observer will detect thermal radiation, and this study aims to provide a method to experimentally confirm it through precise measurement.
AI.method: The research optimizes measurement parameters such as atom-field interaction time, initial atomic state, and measurement basis to reduce estimation uncertainty related to the acceleration factor of the two-level atom.
AI.result: Uncertainty in estimating the acceleration factor is shown to be inversely related to the square root of total probe time, with optimal configurations identified: excited state is best for low acceleration, while ground state is favorable for high acceleration and longer times.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a roadmap for reducing the probe time necessary to test the Unruh effect using atoms with larger transition dipole moments, aiding in experimental verification.

title: Reliability Is Not Free in Universal Quantum Work Extraction
summary: Universal work extraction shows that input-state knowledge is unnecessary to attain the asymptotic free-energy rate. We ask whether this first-order universality extends to reliability, the exponential decay rate of extraction failure. In the work-battery fidelity formulation, we prove that no phase-independent Gibbs-preserving protocol can retain the state-aware Gibbs-preserving exponent throughout a coherent qubit time-translation orbit: at every positive target rate, its worst pointwise exponent is bounded by the corresponding state-aware thermal-operation value. The proof first establishes an exact finite-blocklength identity between phase-robust Gibbs-preserving extraction and state-aware thermal extraction. A trigonometric Remez inequality then upgrades this minimax identity to a pointwise theorem by ruling out exponential localization of the worst phase. For an explicit coherent-qubit family, known-phase Gibbs-preserving extraction is error free, whereas every phase-independent protocol has a finite worst-pointwise exponent. Thus input-state knowledge can be irrelevant to the first-order work rate yet indispensable for optimal exponential reliability.

AI.tldr: The study investigates universal work extraction in quantum systems, focusing on the reliability of extraction protocols. It proves that while input-state knowledge is not necessary for optimal work rates, it is crucial for ensuring low failure rates in extraction processes.
AI.motivation: To explore whether universal work extraction's first-order performance extends to the reliability of extraction in quantum systems.
AI.method: The study employs a proof showing the relationship between phase-robust Gibbs-preserving extraction and state-aware thermal extraction, utilizing a trigonometric Remez inequality for a minimax identity upgrade.
AI.result: The findings indicate that state-independent protocols cannot match the reliability of state-aware ones, as shown through the worst-pointwise exponent constraints in coherent qubit settings.
AI.conclusion: Input-state knowledge, while non-essential for achieving a high work extraction rate, is necessary for maintaining optimal reliability in extraction protocols.

title: Extending the Frontiers of QNLP Beyond English: Grammar-Sensitive Pipeline for Hindi Sentiment Classification Using Compositional Quantum Models
summary: Advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP), whether on classical or quantum platforms, have predominantly focused on English due to its widespread use and abundant linguistic resources. Although English remains the most studied language in computational linguistics, Hindi, the third most spoken language worldwide after Mandarin, has received comparatively limited attention. Spoken primarily in India, Hindi differs significantly from English in its script, syntactic structure, and linguistic characteristics. Hindi uses the Devanagari script, exhibits rich morphological inflection, and follows a subject-object-verb (SOV) word order, unlike English's subject-verb-object (SVO) structure. Motivated by Hindi's linguistic complexity and its underrepresentation in Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP), we propose a grammar-aware QNLP pipeline for Hindi sentiment classification with a focus on sentential negation. We use a manually annotated Hindi sentiment dataset labeled as positive, negative, or neutral, and encode sentences using pregroup grammar types. Sentences are processed with Lambeq to generate quantum circuits using a novel negation-aware compositional grammar. Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks (HQNNs) are trained for both binary and ternary sentiment classification. Our results demonstrate effective sentiment classification and highlight the potential of compositional QNLP for morphologically rich languages.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a grammar-aware quantum natural language processing (QNLP) pipeline for Hindi sentiment classification, addressing its linguistic complexities and underrepresentation in the field.
AI.motivation: Despite being the third most spoken language, Hindi has not been adequately studied in QNLP, prompting the need for focused research on its distinct linguistic features, such as sentential negation and SOV structure.
AI.method: The study employs a manually annotated dataset for Hindi sentiment classification, utilizing pregroup grammar types and a novel negation-aware compositional grammar to generate quantum circuits with Lambeq, followed by training Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks (HQNNs) for binary and ternary sentiment classification.
AI.result: The proposed methodology effectively classifies Hindi sentiment, demonstrating the capabilities of QNLP in handling morphologically rich languages.
AI.conclusion: The research underscores the potential of compositional QNLP to enhance sentiment analysis in languages like Hindi, which have unique grammatical structures.

title: Identity-Paired Progressive Depth Training: When Trainability Persists Beyond Expressibility
summary: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are a leading paradigm for near-term quantum computing, yet their training suffers from sensitivity to circuit depth, initialization, and landscape pathologies such as barren plateaus. We study \emph{progressive depth training} (PDT) -- a layerwise curriculum that trains a shallow circuit before appending new layers -- and identify a fundamental obstacle: fixed entangling gates (CNOTs) in hardware-efficient ansätze cause \emph{initialization shock}, an energy spike when new layers are added. We propose \emph{identity-paired progressive depth training} (IP-PDT), which appends forward/inverse block pairs -- each consisting of a standard rotation$+$CNOT block followed by its reverse -- that compose to the identity at initialization. Because the adjacent CNOT rings cancel, the effective circuit retains only \textit{a single entangling layer} surrounded by \textit{overparameterized local rotations}. We prove a simple \textit{Reachable Set Saturation Theorem}: under this construction the variational manifold expands exactly once (when post-entangler rotations are first introduced) and then \emph{saturates}; all subsequent depth increases provide pure overparameterization of single-qubit unitaries. Despite this saturation, progressive addition of rotation parameters can continue to improve optimization outcomes -- a phenomenon we term \emph{trainability beyond expressibility}. We formalize IP-PDT as a continuation method on nested manifolds, prove monotone energy guarantees under an acceptance rule, and connect energy error to ground-state fidelity through spectral-gap inequalities. A detailed resource analysis shows that IP-PDT achieves lower total gate cost than both baselines by eliminating most CNOT gates.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Identity-Paired Progressive Depth Training (IP-PDT) to mitigate initialization shock in Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) by managing circuit depth and gate usage.
AI.motivation: To address training issues in VQAs caused by circuit depth, initialization, and barren plateaus, specifically focusing on the effects of CNOT gates leading to initialization shock.
AI.method: Proposes IP-PDT, which involves adding forward/inverse block pairs to maintain a single entangling layer surrounded by overparameterized rotations, facilitating a smoother training process.
AI.result: IP-PDT enables optimization to improve despite saturation in the variational manifold, demonstrating trainability beyond expressibility, while achieving lower gate costs by reducing CNOT usage.
AI.conclusion: IP-PDT successfully enhances optimization outcomes in VQAs and reduces gate costs, while providing theoretical guarantees and linking energy error to fidelity through spectral-gap inequalities.

title: Shortcuts to adiabaticity in five-level systems using counter-diabatic driving and time-rescaling optimization
summary: Shortcuts to adiabaticity (STA) is a common protocol to realize high-fidelity and robust quantum control in various quantum systems. To date, STA has been widely applied in two- and three-level systems, whereas designing feasible strategies to achieve perfect quantum state engineering in multi-level systems still remains a challenging task. Here, we propose to use counterdiabatic (CD) driving and time-rescaling (TR) methods to construct multi-state stimulated Raman shortcut-to-adiabatic passage protocols for realizing robust and fast population transfer in chainwise-connected five-state systems. The first protocol is implemented by initially reducing the original five-state system to an equivalent two-state counterpart, and then designing the corresponding driving field by combining CD driving and unitary transformation. Further, we introduce the TR method to optimize the first protocol and thus offers an alternative solution. Numerical calculations show that both protocols can achieve complete population transfer and effectively suppress transient populations of all intermediate states. Compared with the first protocol, the optimized second exhibits better performance within a shorter evolution time.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two protocols using counterdiabatic driving and time-rescaling for efficient population transfer in multi-level quantum systems.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to enhance quantum control and state engineering in multi-level systems, where existing methods have limitations.
AI.method: The authors utilize counterdiabatic driving and time-rescaling techniques to develop two protocols for population transfer in a five-state system, one optimized from an initial two-state reduction.
AI.result: Both protocols successfully achieve complete population transfer while minimizing transient populations of intermediate states, with the optimized protocol showing superior performance in reduced time.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that utilizing CD and TR methods provides effective strategies for robust quantum control in multi-level systems.

title: Removing inhomogeneous broadening in cross-relaxation spectra via hole burning
summary: Quantum relaxometry based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is an easy-to-use technique that detects magnetic noise by measuring the longitudinal relaxation of NV centers. It is favored in chemical and biological applications due to the robustness against imperfect spin control. By tuning the energy level, NV relaxometry can detect magnetic noise generated by other spins and obtain magnetic resonance spectra through cross relaxation. However, the inhomogeneous broadening of NV centers greatly limits the spectral resolution of cross-relaxation spectra. Here we demonstrate a hole-burning technique to remove the inhomogeneous broadening. We utilize a weak pump field to deplete specific NV centers during the relaxation measurement, which contribute a reverse signal in the cross-relaxation spectra with a much narrower linewidth. Our method retains the convenience and sensitivity of NV relaxometry, opening up new avenues for high-resolution magnetic resonance spectroscopy in complex scenarios.

AI.tldr: The study presents a novel hole-burning technique to enhance the spectral resolution in NV center quantum relaxometry by reducing inhomogeneous broadening, facilitating high-resolution magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
AI.motivation: To improve spectral resolution in NV center relaxometry, which is limited by inhomogeneous broadening in typical measurements.
AI.method: The researchers employed a hole-burning technique using a weak pump field to selectively deplete specific NV centers during relaxation measurements, thus narrowing linewidths in the cross-relaxation spectra.
AI.result: The technique successfully produced reverse signals with significantly narrower linewidths, enhancing spectral resolution while maintaining the sensitivity and ease of use of NV relaxometry.
AI.conclusion: This advancement opens new possibilities for high-resolution magnetic resonance spectroscopy in complex chemical and biological environments.

title: Geometric Qubits in Programmable Atomic Trimers
summary: Motivated by programmable tweezer arrays, we develop an exactly solvable shape-space theory for near-equilateral atomic trimers. The Higgs oscillator on Kendall's shape sphere gives a nonresonant spectral lattice whose fixed-angular-momentum relative-stationary minimizers are supported on two adjacent admissible sites. These symmetry-selected doublets are separated from higher relative-stationary branches by a finite branch gap. With phase-coherent shape-mode driving and Rydberg-mediated conditional phases, they furnish a candidate route to geometric qubits and entangling operations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a shape-space theory for atomic trimers, using the Higgs oscillator to create a lattice structure that has implications for quantum computing.
AI.motivation: To enhance programmable tweezer arrays for applications in quantum computing.
AI.method: Employs an exactly solvable shape-space theory and explores the behavior of atomic trimers on Kendall's shape sphere, focusing on spectral characteristics and symmetry properties.
AI.result: The study identifies fixed-angular-momentum stationary states organized in symmetry-selected doublets, with a finite branch gap from higher states.
AI.conclusion: These findings provide a potential framework for geometric qubits and entanglement in quantum operations.

title: Attosecond delay metrology beyond the photon coherence time with spectrally resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry
summary: Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interferometry enables delay estimation at the quantum precision limit but is traditionally constrained to path differences within the coherence time of the interfering photons. Here, we demonstrate single-measurement path-delay sensing at the measurement Cramer-Rao bound using spectrally resolved HOM interference, thereby removing the conventional dynamic-range limitation imposed by the photon coherence window, with no scanning required for calibration. By extracting delay information from the spectral interference fringes of spectrally entangled photon pairs, we retain near-optimal sensitivity over an operational range exceeding the photon coherence time by over two orders of magnitude. Using one million detected photon pairs, we achieve a time-delay precision of 20 attosecond (6 nm), while real-time operation (at 1 Hz) yields 330 attosecond (100 nm) precision. Because the estimator relies on fringe periodicity rather than absolute coincidence rates, the method is intrinsically robust to photon losses and variations in interference visibility, eliminating the need for recalibration. As a practical demonstration, we measure the thickness of a 300 um transmissive target with nanometer-scale precision. These results mark a significant step towards deploying quantum-limited measurements in real-world sensing applications using HOM interferometry.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method for single-measurement path-delay sensing in Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry, surpassing conventional coherence limits and achieving high precision without recalibration.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of traditional HOM interferometry related to coherence time and dynamic-range, enabling more effective quantum precision measurements in real-world applications.
AI.method: Using spectrally resolved HOM interference to extract delay information from spectral fringes of entangled photon pairs, allowing for sensitive measurements beyond the coherence time.
AI.result: Achieved a time-delay precision of 20 attoseconds (6 nm) using one million photon pairs, with real-time operation yielding 330 attoseconds (100 nm) precision.
AI.conclusion: The technique demonstrates significant advancements for quantum-limited measurements in practical sensing applications, exemplified by measuring the thickness of a 300 um target with nanometer precision.

title: Universal Parent Hamiltonians for Adiabatic Warm Starts
summary: Computing the ground state properties of quantum systems is an important potential application of quantum computing. The success probability of quantum phase estimation approaches to ground state problems is proportional to the overlap of the input state with the ground state. Local ansatz state approaches suffer from the orthogonality catastrophe, whereas adiabatic state preparation (ASP) can prepare good approximations with a cost growing with the inverse square of the minimum spectral gap along the adiabatic path. When the initial and target Hamiltonians lie in quantum phases separated by a first order phase transition, the minimum spectral gap along the adiabatic path becomes exponentially small as a function of system size. We pursue a solution to this problem based on choosing an initial Hamiltonian for adiabatic state preparation whose ground state lies in the same quantum phase as the target ground state. We develop a protocol for universal adiabatic warm starts with universal parent Hamiltonians (UPHAWS) that can initialize ASP in any state whose preparation circuit is known. We use the Feynman--Kitaev clock Hamiltonian as a universal parent Hamiltonian, for preparation circuits with and without mid circuit measurement. We benchmark the framework on a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric matrix product state (MPS) family interpolating to a target GHZ Hamiltonian, and on the linear $H_6$ chain under symmetric bond stretching. For the $H_6$ system a bond-dimension-$4$ matrix product state warm-start increases the minimum gap on the adiabatic path by a factor of two relative to the Hartree-Fock initialization. To perform these classical benchmark simulations we develop a momentum-space truncation of the adiabatic Hamiltonian that may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a novel protocol for adiabatic state preparation to address issues with ground state properties in quantum systems, using universal parent Hamiltonians to improve preparation efficiency.
AI.motivation: The study is motivated by the challenges of preparing ground states in quantum computing, particularly when facing orthogonality catastrophe and exponential scaling of spectral gaps in first order phase transitions.
AI.method: The authors propose a universal adiabatic warm start method (UPHAWS) that selects initial Hamiltonians aligned with the target ground state phase, utilizing the Feynman-Kitaev clock Hamiltonian.
AI.result: The UPHAWS method demonstrates significant improvements, such as a two-fold increase in minimum gap for the $H_6$ chain compared to traditional initialization methods.
AI.conclusion: This framework shows promise for enhancing adiabatic state preparation by utilizing well-defined initial states, potentially advancing quantum computing applications.

title: Experimental Nanoscale Thermodynamics
summary: Modern fabrication techniques have allowed artificial systems to be constructed on a nanometre length scale. The ideas underlying thermodynamics, a field invented to describe large macroscopic systems, need to be modified to describe much smaller systems. There are implications for our understanding of entropy, cooling, the arrow of time, heat flow, engines, erasure, and mutual information. The theoretical concepts have been implemented and tested in a wide range of experiments, many of which are at low temperatures. Nanoscale thermodynamics is not only a descriptive tool of nanoscale systems, but a design principle that helps us to build new architectures, processors and learning machines.

AI.tldr: Nanometre-scale fabrication requires modifications to thermodynamic concepts for small systems, influencing various fundamental properties and enabling new technological advancements.
AI.motivation: To adapt thermodynamic principles originally designed for macroscopic systems to the nanoscale, addressing phenomena like entropy and heat flow in smaller systems.
AI.method: Application and testing of modified theoretical concepts in a variety of experimental setups, particularly at low temperatures.
AI.result: These adaptations have led to practical implementations in nanoscale architectures, processors, and learning machines.
